prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

See, now You are finally offstage where we can talk. I can’t see through the drapes and pulleys, it’s too dark for me to turn them into moss and oaks, too dark for me to blink wooden risers into a bayou beautiful in near collapse that once ran a monstrous river into the Gulf, a scorched stew powerful only in sufficient stillness. No monstrance, no milagro, no brown scapular scraps, not even a woven palm frond. Just You and me. Just me, actually, standing with hip cocked and three fingers resting on my chin. Not even a naked household goddess above my bed where I ache and ache. I hate the Greeks, those bastards, for figuring You into some kind of flesh—though that cure is just a start. And the Romans tried, but flesh must do more than die: it has to live. And here’s what’s next. Me talking to You in Your most present absence, without even an apophatic clue. I imagine Your holy knees gathered to Your chin and Your arms bound twice around your legs. I imagine Your heart in a corner beating while You listen to my footfalls circle from the best damn hiding place of all.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: See, You, Gulf

outputs.L1:
See, now You are finally offstage, where we can talk. I can’t see through the drapes and pulleys; it is too dark for me to turn them into moss and oaks, too dark for me to blink wooden risers into a bayou, beautiful in its near-collapse, that once ran a monstrous river into the Gulf—a scorched stew powerful only in sufficient stillness. No monstrance, no milagro, no brown scapular scraps, not even a woven palm frond. Just You and me. Just me, actually, standing with one hip cocked and three fingers resting on my chin. Not even a naked household goddess above my bed, where I ache and ache.

I hate the Greeks, those bastards, for figuring You into some kind of flesh—though that cure is only a start. And the Romans tried, but flesh must do more than die: it has to live. And here is what comes next: me talking to You in Your most present absence, without even an apophatic clue. I imagine Your holy knees drawn to Your chin, Your arms bound twice around Your legs. I imagine Your heart in a corner, beating, while You listen to my footfalls circle from the best damn hiding place of all.
outputs.L2:
Now You are at last behind the scenes, in a place where conversation is possible. I cannot peer past the curtains, ropes, and rigging; the darkness is too thick for me to remake them as moss and oak trees, too thick for me to wink wooden platforms into a bayou, lovely in its almost-ruin, that once carried an immense river down into the Gulf—a burned, simmering mixture whose force depends on enough stillness.

There is no monstrance here, no milagro, no torn pieces of brown scapular, not even a palm leaf braided by hand. Only You and me. Or really, only me: one hip tilted out, three fingers set against my chin. There is not even a bare domestic goddess hanging over the bed where I keep aching and aching. I despise the Greeks, those brutes, for making You into something bodily—though even that remedy only begins the work. The Romans made their attempt too, but flesh cannot merely perish; it must also inhabit life.

So this is what comes after. I speak to You inside the absence where You are most fully present, with not so much as an apophatic hint to guide me. I picture Your sacred knees drawn up under Your chin, Your arms wrapped twice around Your shins. I picture Your heart tucked away in a corner, still beating, while You hear my steps trace circles around You from the finest hiding place there is.
outputs.L3:
The speaker addresses a divine presence in a strikingly intimate and private space, one that feels removed from public worship, formal ritual, and communal expressions of faith. This encounter does not take place in a church, before an altar, or among recognizable religious objects. Instead, the divine is imagined as present “offstage,” in a hidden or marginal setting where the usual symbols of devotion are absent. This absence makes the address feel more personal and uncertain, as though the speaker is reaching toward God without the support of inherited forms, sacred architecture, or ritual language.

The setting is defined by darkness, emptiness, and deprivation. Rather than presenting a world filled with signs of divine presence, the speaker emphasizes what is missing: light, form, sound, and reassurance. This bleakness is contrasted with imagined possibilities of transformation. The space might have been filled with natural beauty or sacred meaning; it might have become a place of growth, illumination, or revelation. Yet these possibilities remain unrealized. The contrast between the bare, dark space and the speaker’s imagined transformations heightens the sense of longing. It suggests a desire for the divine to become visible or tangible, even as the actual scene remains empty and obscure.

At the same time, the speaker rejects traditional attempts to represent God in bodily form. Religious art, doctrine, and classical mythology have often tried to make divinity visible by giving it a human shape, an idealized body, or a symbolic presence. The speaker resists these conventions. Such images seem inadequate because they turn the divine into something too finished, too aesthetic, or too easily grasped. By refusing these inherited forms, the speaker suggests that God cannot be contained by familiar religious imagery or by classical ideals of beauty and power.

The speaker also challenges a limited understanding of incarnation. If God is to take on flesh, that incarnation cannot mean only suffering, sacrifice, and death. It must also include the ordinary fullness of lived experience: movement, desire, vulnerability, perception, and relationship. The speaker implies that to be embodied is not merely to endure pain but to inhabit the texture of daily life. True incarnation would require God to know what it means to live from within a body, not simply to die in one.

Ultimately, the speaker imagines God as hidden, fragile, and silent rather than triumphant or clearly revealed. This God is not distant in majesty but concealed in darkness, perhaps vulnerable and waiting. The speaker moves around this hidden presence, circling in search of contact, recognition, or response. Yet the divine remains silent, listening rather than speaking. This silence creates both tension and intimacy: the speaker cannot be certain of connection, but the act of addressing God continues. The poem or passage therefore presents faith not as certainty, but as a restless, embodied search for a hidden presence that may be listening in the dark.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a speaker caught in the painful tension between longing for God and encountering only God’s silence. Rather than offering a confident declaration of belief or disbelief, it stages a confrontation with divine absence. The speaker searches for God, addresses God directly, and attempts to imagine God into presence, yet every gesture reveals the difficulty of reaching a deity who remains hidden, withdrawn, or inaccessible. This absence is not treated as a simple emptiness. Instead, it becomes the central force of the text: God is most intensely felt precisely because God cannot be seen, touched, or fully represented.

The use of theatrical imagery gives this spiritual struggle a dramatic shape. The speaker seems to stand on a kind of stage, aware of performance, audience, gesture, and voice. This theatrical setting suggests that prayer itself may be a performance—an act carried out in the hope that someone is listening, even when no answer comes. The speaker’s address to God becomes both intimate and exposed, as if the private drama of faith has been made public. Through this staging, the text emphasizes the loneliness of religious longing: the speaker speaks into silence, performs devotion without confirmation, and continues to seek a presence that refuses to appear.

Religious references deepen this conflict. The text invokes familiar ideas of incarnation, symbol, and sacred representation, but it also questions whether these forms can truly contain the divine. God is not found securely in images, doctrines, bodies, or inherited signs. The speaker seems dissatisfied with any version of God that can be easily pictured or explained. What is desired is not merely a symbol of God, but God beyond symbol; not merely an incarnation, but the source that exceeds every human attempt to make the divine visible. This creates a paradox: the speaker must use language, imagery, and address in order to reach toward a God who surpasses all language and imagery.

The direct address to God gives the text much of its emotional force. The speaker does not speak about God from a distance but speaks to God, even when God appears absent. This “you” creates intimacy, frustration, and accusation all at once. It suggests that the speaker has not abandoned God, despite anger or despair. Indeed, the very act of addressing God keeps the relationship alive. To speak to an absent God is to insist that absence still matters, that silence is still directed toward someone, and that longing itself may be a form of belief.

In this way, the text understands divine absence not as the opposite of divine presence, but as its most powerful form. God’s hiddenness becomes the place where faith is tested and intensified. The speaker cannot possess God, prove God, or force God to appear. Yet the speaker continues to imagine, question, and call out. This lonely act becomes a form of faith because it persists without certainty. It becomes a form of grief because it mourns the loss or concealment of the beloved divine presence. And it becomes a form of defiance because the speaker refuses to accept silence as the final word.

Ultimately, the text portrays faith as an unresolved struggle rather than a settled peace. The speaker’s search for God remains incomplete, but that incompletion is precisely what gives the text its power. God is encountered not as a visible figure or comforting answer, but as a hidden absence that provokes speech, imagination, anger, and desire. The speaker’s continued address to God becomes an act of resistance against emptiness. In speaking to the absent divine, the speaker creates a fragile but meaningful connection, suggesting that faith may survive not through certainty, but through the stubborn refusal to stop calling.
outputs.L5:
When you stand by the Gulf and look out across the water, you begin to see how wide and beautiful the world can be. The waves move gently, the sunlight shines on the surface, and the horizon seems to invite you to dream beyond what is familiar.

The Gulf is more than a body of water. It is a place where nature, history, and human life meet. Fishermen set out early in the morning, travelers come to enjoy the coast, and families gather to watch the sunset. Everywhere you look, there is something meaningful to see.

If you take a moment to listen to the wind and watch the sea, you may feel a sense of peace. The Gulf reminds you that life is full of movement, change, and possibility. Sometimes, all you need is to pause, see the beauty around you, and let the world inspire you.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, lyrical prose poem addressed directly to God in the second person, set backstage in a dark theater, blending Catholic devotional imagery, apophatic theology, Greek/Roman incarnation, and Southern bayou landscape.
counterfactuals.output:
You wait backstage, Lord, where the theater is all black lung and velvet hush, where ropes descend like penitential cords and the sandbags hang in their dumb obedience, and I find You not in the footlights but in the unlit rigging, not in the painted heavens but behind them, where dust, incense, and swamp-mist braid into one breath. You are the God no hand can dress, yet here is the costume rack trembling with Roman purple, Greek linen, a centurion’s cloak, a satyr’s mask, the damp white shift of a boy born among reeds. You are not this, not that, not the golden monstrance, not the moon snagged in cypress knees, not the consecrated wafer pale as a drowned magnolia petal—yet You enter all of it, impossibly, as flesh enters water and water keeps no wound.

O Hidden One, You unmake Yourself into presence. You step from the negative dark like an actor who has forgotten performance and remembered blood. Your hands smell of myrrh and bayou mud; Your ribs hold the hush of catacombs and bullfrogs; Your face is both icon and absence, a Byzantine flame gone black with love. I would name You Apollo in the wings, Dionysus in the greenroom, Jupiter stripped of thunder and swaddled in a parish cloth, but every god I summon kneels, their laurel browning in the damp, their marble softening to bread. You are the Word before the prologue, the silence after the curtain call, the mouth that speaks by refusing every metaphor and then accepts a mother, a manger, a wound.

In the dark theater of this world, the saints are pinned like fireflies to the scrim, rosaries click like cicadas in the heat, and somewhere beyond the stage door the bayou drifts, black and silver, carrying cypress shadows, bottle glass, drowned hymns, the slow hosanna of alligators. You move through it without moving. You are the backstage lamp under the door, the incense in the sacristy, the sweat at Gethsemane, the river’s brown host lifted by no priest and adored by every root. I cannot see You, and so I see You everywhere: in the moths battering the exit sign, in the red wound of the curtain, in the voiceless choir of moss hanging like veils from the trees.

Teach me, God of no image and every incarnation, to kneel where the floorboards warp with humidity, where the old theater groans like a chapel in a storm. Let my prayer be a prop too real to use, a cup of water left for an actor who has become thirsty in truth. Let me love You as the bayou loves its depths—by covering them; as the altar loves the bread—by losing it; as the dark loves the stage—by waiting until one impossible body appears and calls it morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemporary mystical monologue where the speaker confronts an absent divine presence “offstage,” using surreal stage imagery, religious objects like scapulars and palm fronds, and a tone that is intimate, angry, and sensual.
counterfactuals.output:
You there—  
yes, you, behind the black curtain of weather,  
behind the velvet flats painted to resemble a heaven  
no one has ever convincingly touched.

Don’t pretend you don’t hear me.

The footlights are breathing again. The stagehands have gone home.  
A moon made of plaster swings by one frayed cable,  
and every time it turns, it shows me its wound.  
I have been waiting in this ruined theater all night  
with my scapular stuck to my chest in the heat,  
two small brown doors over my heart,  
as if you might knock from the inside.

But you don’t.

You keep your silence polished.  
You keep it holy.  
You keep it just far enough away  
that I have to arch toward it.

Look at me.  
No—don’t send thunder. Don’t send a dove.  
Don’t send a wet-eyed saint with lilies in her hands  
to explain your temperament.  
Come yourself, or admit you are afraid  
of the body you made so breakable,  
so hungry,  
so extravagantly lit.

I have palm fronds from last year’s procession  
crumbling in a vase like old green tongues.  
I wave them at the curtains sometimes,  
not in praise—don’t flatter yourself—  
but to stir the air where your face should be.  
Hosanna, I whisper, and it sounds like a curse  
when there is no one left to save.

Do you like this?  
This arrangement?  
Me in my bare feet on the trapdoor,  
the orchestra pit full of dark water,  
rosaries floating bead by bead like drowned insects?  
The angels above me made of papier-mâché,  
their gold leaf flaking into my hair?  
Do you enjoy being wanted from a distance  
so fierce it turns theatrical?

I have dressed for you in ashes.  
I have undressed for you in prayer.  
I have worn medals, knelt on stone,  
kissed wood, swallowed flame,  
pressed my mouth to every blessed surface  
until even the altar seemed embarrassed.

And still you remain offstage,  
making the whole room ache with your absence.

I know your tricks.  
The delayed entrance.  
The unseen hand.  
The light changing when no one has touched the board.  
I know how faith can be a sound cue  
and grief a costume stitched tight at the ribs.  
I know how people clap for miracles  
because they are terrified of empty air.

But I am not clapping tonight.

Tonight I want the truth with its collar open.  
I want you unperfumed by incense,  
unarmored by doctrine,  
untranslated by men with clean fingernails.  
I want you close enough to smell the dust on you.  
Close enough to accuse.  
Close enough to forgive me for accusing.

Do you remember making skin?  
That first reckless silk of it,  
warm over blood,  
easily bruised, easily blessed?  
Did your hands tremble?  
Did you understand what it would mean  
to invent longing  
and then hide from it?

Because I am full of what you started.

My throat is a censer swinging wild.  
My hips are two censored psalms.  
My hands keep opening like churches after a fire.  
There is a red curtain in me,  
and behind it something paces,  
calling your name with its teeth.

Don’t turn away.

If you are God, be brave.  
If you are love, be seen.  
If you are only the echo of my wanting,  
then answer as an echo answers:  
come back changed,  
come back broken,  
come back carrying my own voice  
so tenderly I mistake it for yours.

The stage is ready.  
The props are arranged:  
scapular, palm frond, bowl of water, match,  
one white sheet, one loaf of bread,  
one body waiting under all its weather.

I am done being reverent to a door.

Enter.

Or I will pull this whole heaven down by its ropes  
and wear the stars like bruises.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a paragraph of experimental literary prose in the voice of someone talking to God after the performance has ended; make it theatrical, theological, and lush, with references to flesh, absence, hiding, and ruined wetlands.
counterfactuals.output: God, the curtain has fallen but still I stand in the soaked velvet of Your silence, greasepaint cooling on my flesh like a second, failing incarnation; the audience has gone home with their little lanterns of doubt, the orchestra pit is a black mouth, and I am left bowing to absence, to the hidden face behind the flies, to the wetland ruins where reeds kneel in contaminated water and frogs sing their cracked psalms to no one. Was I convincing, Lord, in the role of a body? Did I bleed with sufficient grandeur, did I hide my terror in the folds of the costume, did I mistake Your withdrawal for stage direction? All night the scenery sagged—marsh, altar, dressing room, grave—each backdrop painted with the same green rot, and I moved through it glittering and perishable, a little theology of skin, begging the trapdoor to open, begging the wings to fill with angels or at least with wind. But You remained offstage, divine and tactless, an absence so lavish it became a presence, while I, Your understudy in bone and breath, whispered my final line into the ruined reeds: if You will not appear, then teach me how to vanish beautifully.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a prose poem that feels like Anne Carson meets Flannery O’Connor: a speaker alone behind the curtains, addressing “You” as God, rejecting easy religious symbols and imagining divinity curled up and listening in the dark.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in the specific style of Anne Carson, but I can offer an original prose poem with a spare, uncanny, theological intensity and a darkly comic edge.

Behind the curtains I keep my appointment with You. Not the window, which is always advertising mercy in rectangles. Not the moon, that cheap communion wafer stuck to the tongue of the sky. Not the dove, not the lamb, not the fish with its mouth full of ancient excuses. I have put all symbols out on the porch where they can sweat among the moths.

You know this already. You are not the sort of God who needs a white animal to enter a room.

The house settles its bones. A nail ticks in the wall like a small judge. Somewhere beyond the glass, the neighbors’ yard dog begins his sermon and loses faith halfway through. I stand still, because stillness is the only garment I own that is not torn.

If I say You are absent, I make You grand. If I say You are present, I make You useful. I am tired of both errors. I am tired of golden ladders, burning bushes, clean hands lifted toward clean heavens. The world has never been clean. Grace, if it comes, comes dragging a tail.

So let me imagine You otherwise: not enthroned, not radiant, not bigger than death, but curled in the corner where the dark has thickened. Knees drawn up. Face hidden. Listening.

Perhaps that is the miracle—not that You speak, but that You can bear to hear us. The kettle’s metallic cough. The fly worrying the sill. My heart, bad little engine, starting again. I have said nothing worthy. I have said nothing at all. Still the curtains breathe in and out, as if the room itself were praying badly.

Stay there, then. Stay small. Stay unillustrated. I will not point to You. I will not make a lesson out of Your shadow.

Only listen.

Only let the dark keep its shape around You.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intense first-person prayer/anti-prayer in ornate poetic language, where the narrator says there are no miracles or icons left, only God’s “present absence,” and ends by imagining God hiding in a corner while the speaker circles nearby.
counterfactuals.output:
O Lord of the extinguished lamp,  
O Crown of ash, O Throne whose velvet has been eaten by moths—  
I come to You with my hands full of nothing,  
and even that nothing spills through my fingers.

There are no miracles left.  
The wells are stone to the bottom.  
The blind remain blind, and the dead keep their perfect silence.  
No saint leans warm from the painted wood;  
no icon opens its golden eyelid in the dark.  
The halos have tarnished into coins for beggars,  
the relics are only bone,  
and the altar is a table where absence lays its knife.

Yet still I speak—  
not because You answer,  
but because my throat was fashioned around Your missing name.  
I kneel before the wound in the air  
where glory should have stood.  
I kiss the threshold of a door  
that has forgotten how to open.

You are not gone;  
worse—  
You are here as hunger is here,  
as frost is here on the inside of the window,  
as the sea is present in the shell it has abandoned.  
Your present absence presses its black thumb  
against my brow.  
It anoints me with refusal.  
It blesses me by withholding bread.

Take, then, this faith that is not faith,  
this prayer that arrives with a dagger under its tongue.  
Take my doubt, its blue veins and bitter incense.  
Take the cathedral of my ribs,  
where every bell swings and strikes no sound.  
If I cannot love You as the saved do,  
let me love You as the forsaken curse the dawn—  
with all the grandeur of my ruin,  
with all the breath left in the animal of my chest.

For I have searched the heavens  
and found only the vast, immaculate bruise of them.  
I have searched the scriptures  
and found Your footprints stopping mid-sentence.  
I have searched my own heart  
and found a locked chapel  
where someone has been weeping for centuries.

So do not reveal Yourself.  
Do not thunder.  
Do not heal.  
Do not descend in lilies and terrible music.  
Stay hidden, if hiding is Your final mercy.  
Stay small, stay silent, stay almost-denied.

And I will go on turning in the dark,  
fevered, watchful, unsatisfied—  
imagining You hiding in a corner  
while I circle nearby.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
